title: Graphic Designer
oneLiner: Generation is free now. Choosing, and defending the choice, is the whole job.
summary: The bottom of this market is gone and is not coming back: the social post, the flyer, the fifteenth banner variant, the stock illustration. A model produces forty options in a minute, and the client who used to pay for one is now paying for none. What survives sits above that line — deciding what a brand should look like, judging which of the forty options is right and why, and taking responsibility for a visual system that has to hold together across years and channels. The gap widens: designers with taste and an argument are more productive than they have ever been, while designers who competed on execution speed are competing against something free.

tasks.name: Social posts, banners, resizes
tasks.note: Templates plus generation killed this tier. The client does it themselves in the time it takes to write your brief.

tasks.name: Stock illustration & spot imagery
tasks.note: Generated on demand, in the exact style requested, at zero marginal cost.

tasks.name: Layout & production artwork
tasks.note: Tools auto-compose and auto-adapt. A designer still fixes what the machine does not see — but in minutes, not days.

tasks.name: Concept development
tasks.note: AI is an excellent divergence engine and a poor convergence one. It floods you with directions; picking the right one is unchanged.

tasks.name: Brand identity & visual systems
tasks.note: A system that must survive ten channels and five years, and be defensible to a board. Coherence over time is not a prompt.

tasks.name: Art direction & critique
tasks.note: The value is the rejection. Knowing why three of forty options are right, and being able to say so out loud, is what clients actually buy.

tasks.name: Client persuasion & stakeholder work
tasks.note: Most design work dies in a meeting, not in the file. Defending an idea to a nervous client is the job nobody automates.

whatSurvives: Judgment and the argument behind it — generating options was never the scarce part.
adaptPrompt:
You are my design collaborator. You widen the option space; I decide and I direct.

Context I will give you: the brand, the audience, the medium, the constraint I cannot break, and the feeling the work has to produce.

What I want from you:
1. Six distinct directions — actually distinct, not one idea in six colourways. For each: the core visual idea in one sentence, the reference world it draws from, and who it will alienate. That last part matters; work that alienates nobody says nothing.
2. For the direction I pick: expand it into a system. Type pairing with a reason, palette with a reason, spacing logic, image treatment, and how it degrades on a small screen or in one colour.
3. A critique pass on my work when I share it. Be specific and structural — hierarchy, contrast, rhythm, alignment. 'Looks good' is worthless to me; tell me what is fighting what.
4. The argument I will need in the client meeting: why this choice serves their stated objective, in their language, not in design language.

Rules: never tell me something works because it is 'modern' or 'clean'. Give the mechanism. When I am about to make a safe, boring choice, say so plainly.
